idiom_name: AsyncLocalStorage<RequestContext> from node:async_hooks behind typed helpers
implementation_notes: TypeScript defines no storage mechanism of its own - types are erased - so the realization is the runtime's: in Node, AsyncLocalStorage<T> gives a typed store bound to the asynchronous execution chain, and the TypeScript contribution is the shape around it, a typed store instance, a run()/withContext helper and an accessor whose return type is explicitly T | undefined so callers must handle the no-context case. The classic key/collection/proxy structure is replaced by the store object plus run(), with the type parameter acting as the proxy. In the browser there is no equivalent ambient store (module state is per realm and Worker globals are separate realms), so request context must be passed explicitly; in Node every worker thread owns separate store instances.
pitfalls: getStore() returns RequestContext | undefined: a typed accessor that throws when no context is active turns a silent undefined into a failure that surfaces immediately, but the type system cannot prove the caller is inside run().

Type-only reasoning misleads here: the store is a runtime object bound to the async chain, so awaits inside run() keep it while work that escapes the chain (unawaited promises, event listeners, worker threads) silently loses it.

Declaration merging to attach context to framework request types (declare global { namespace Express { interface Request { context: RequestContext } } }) reintroduces the plumbing and keeps the same lifetime pitfalls, while the type vanishes at runtime.
Each worker thread owns separate AsyncLocalStorage instances, so context must cross the boundary as a message and be re-entered with run() inside the worker.
